**"when you said, “We hear and obey.”"** states the believer's response to Allah's commands and prohibitions. The pledge applies when obedience is welcome and when it is difficult, in ease and hardship, not only when it agrees with personal preference.

**"And be mindful of Allah."** Taqwa means guarding against disobedience out of awareness of Him. Here it especially requires fidelity to the covenant, carrying out what is commanded and avoiding what is forbidden. There is no condition in which betrayal becomes hidden from the One who took the pledge.

**"Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart"** includes loyalty and treachery before they are visible in action. He knows concealed thoughts and intentions. Outward words of obedience cannot conceal inward refusal from Him.

### What did the pledge require?

The pledge to the Messenger ﷺ included hearing and obeying in energetic and reluctant moments, even when others were preferred in the distribution of rights. It also included not contesting leadership with those entitled to it. The reminder presents obedience as a commitment extending beyond moments of personal satisfaction.

Another verse joins the Messenger's call to belief with the covenant already taken (57:8). The connection makes the present command a summons to fulfil an accepted responsibility, not merely to admire the idea of faith.

A further interpretation, reported from Ibn 'Abbas, takes this as a reminder to the Jews of their undertaking to follow Muhammad ﷺ and adhere to his law. That reading is preserved alongside the explanation concerning Muslims' pledge. Both give the covenant practical consequences.

### How does faith shape the inward response?

Faith is described as a bond between Allah and His servant. The servant undertakes to live in awareness of Him, and Allah provides guardianship in this life and the next. The first expression of fidelity is steadfastness toward the Lord in the whole pattern of life.

Looking at the universe should awaken recognition of His greatness and power. Looking at oneself should awaken awareness of His grace and mercy. Love, fear and concern should take their direction from Him. Prayer, remembrance, obedience and spending for His cause express that orientation, and devotion should become a source of willing joy rather than mere outward compliance.

The covenant also requires justice toward other people. The following verse develops that duty, especially when resentment makes fairness difficult. Here the emphasis remains on the faithful heart from which both worship and just dealings should proceed.

### In short

- Guidance to Islam and the sending of the Messenger ﷺ are favours to remember with gratitude.
- The covenant requires genuine hearing and obedience, including when personal preference or advantage points elsewhere.
- Fidelity includes inward loyalty as well as outward conduct, because Allah knows concealed intentions.
- A life centred on Allah should bear fruit in worship, remembrance and just treatment of others.

8.text:
Allah commands believers to act for His sake and uphold justice: "O believers! Stand firm for Allah and bear true testimony." The instruction reaches the hardest case, an enemy whose conduct has caused anger or injury. Hatred must not become permission to distort evidence, withhold another person's right or inflict a new wrong.

Faithfulness to the covenant includes both devotion to Allah and fair dealings with people. Justice gives a person what is due, neither more nor less according to personal affection or resentment. The verse makes that standard a duty before the One who knows every action.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Stand firm for Allah"** means persist in fulfilling His rights and seeking His pleasure. The motive is not reputation, popularity or the approval of people. A person standing for Allah cannot rightly use that claim to excuse oppression.

**"and bear true testimony."** Witnesses must speak honestly and justly. Shahadah, testimony, helps those deciding a matter reach a sound judgment. It must not be turned into a weapon for a preferred side or hidden when its truth becomes inconvenient.

**"Do not let the hatred of a people lead you to injustice."** The command includes hostile disbelievers as well as anyone personally disliked. A specific gloss mentions resentment toward Shurayh Ibn Shurahbil and warns against injustice to the pilgrims of Bakr Ibn Wa'il. The wider instruction is to refuse aggression even where grievance is real.

**"Be just! That is closer to righteousness."** Taqwa is awareness of Allah expressed through obedience. Justice belongs to it, while oppression contradicts it. "Closer" does not offer injustice as another acceptable religious option. It emphasises the relationship between fairness and genuine fear of Allah.

**"And be mindful of Allah. Surely Allah is All-Aware of what you do"** repeats the inward safeguard. No act of fairness or unfairness is hidden from Him. He will repay the person according to what was actually done, not according to the justification offered to other people.

### Why compare this with the command in Surah Al-Nisa'?

The instruction there places justice prominently and requires truthful witness even against oneself, parents and relatives (4:135). Here the words first emphasise standing for Allah and then justice, before forbidding hatred from producing unfairness. The different emphasis is explained through two common obstacles.

One obstacle is affection for oneself and one's circle. A person may imagine that protecting family or friends is itself an act for Allah. Placing justice first prevents that claim from excusing partiality. A concession that violates justice cannot be justified merely by naming a good relationship.

The other obstacle is hostility. A person who begins with the requirement to stand for Allah must recognise that His claim reaches the treatment of enemies too. Hatred cannot set aside a duty owed to Him. Both word orders lead to the same requirement, but approach different temptations.

The two verses therefore prohibit opposite forms of bias. Neither protecting a friend nor injuring an enemy is a sufficient reason to depart from the truth. They also require people to supply honest evidence rather than make a judge or other decision-maker work without the facts.

### Does nearer to piety imply that injustice has some piety?

No. The comparative expression stresses the right course without making the opposite course acceptable. Another cited Qur'anic expression describes the people of Paradise as having the better dwelling and resting place. It does not need to grant goodness to the alternative in order to express their good position.

A similar point appears in words spoken by some female Companions to 'Umar. They called him more stern than the Messenger ﷺ. Their meaning was to describe 'Umar's sternness, not to attribute harshness to the Prophet ﷺ. Language of comparison does not always imply that both sides share the quality in the same way.

Here justice is the course required by taqwa. The person cannot choose oppression and then argue that it is merely a little less close to piety. The verse has already forbidden that choice.

### Can a witness refuse to endorse an unjust gift?

An-Nu'man bin Bashir reports in the Two Sahihs that his father gave him a gift. His mother, 'Amrah bint Rawahah, would not agree unless the Messenger ﷺ witnessed it. His father therefore approached the Prophet ﷺ.

The Prophet ﷺ asked whether all his children had received an equivalent gift. When the answer was no, he instructed him to fear Allah and treat his children equally. He refused to witness injustice. An-Nu'man's father then withdrew the gift.

The report shows that testimony is not an empty ceremonial signature. A person asked to attest something must consider whether the act being endorsed is just. The Prophet's ﷺ refusal connects the witness's responsibility with the rights of those affected.

### Why must witnesses also be protected from harm?

Surah Al-Baqarah forbids concealing testimony and describes the concealing heart as sinful (2:283). Giving true evidence is therefore wajib, a binding duty. Yet that duty is accompanied by an instruction that neither scribe nor witness should be harmed (2:282). A system demanding evidence must not punish honest people for supplying it.

The social criticism here describes repeated police and court appearances, pointless delay and hostile examination designed to break witnesses rather than establish truth. The witness loses working time and faces trouble for an event he did not cause. After such an experience, he may resolve never to come forward again.

The result is a destructive cycle. People who actually saw an event avoid being identified, and fabricated witnesses fill the gap. Courts then decide on the material presented to them, however unreliable. The passage expresses the severity of this failure by saying that not even five or ten percent of cases in the system being criticised reach a just outcome. That is its polemical assessment of the setting it describes, not a new statistical claim about courts today.

It attributes much of the procedure to the inherited British colonial system and contrasts it with the simpler, faster justice it describes in the Hijaz and elsewhere. The practical proposal is to restructure evidence-taking around the two Qur'anic duties together: the person who knows the truth must speak, and the authorities must avoid unnecessary hardship to him.

Witnesses should be treated well and released as soon as their evidence has been properly recorded. Truthful testimony is less likely to disappear where giving it does not threaten a person's livelihood. Protecting witnesses serves justice rather than weakening it.

### Does testimony only mean speaking in court?

No. Shahadah in the Qur'an and Sunnah is broader than a formal court appearance. It includes statements on which others rely to make decisions about rights, qualifications or responsibilities.

A medical certificate declaring someone unfit for duty or fit for retirement on health grounds is testimony. If it knowingly misstates the person's condition, it becomes false evidence. The fact that it appears on a familiar administrative form does not remove its moral seriousness.

Marking an examination also testifies to a student's performance. Deliberately changing the marks, or carelessly giving an inaccurate assessment, falls under the same warning. The people affected depend on the marker's honesty and attention.

A graduation certificate or professional testimonial states that its recipient has the ability the document claims. If that ability is absent, the signatories have endorsed something untrue. Their responsibility cannot be dismissed as routine paperwork.

These examples extend the verse's demand into ordinary institutions. The witness must consider what his statement actually tells others, not simply whether the statement carries the formal label of testimony.

### What does the discussion say about voting?

It treats a vote as having three aspects. First, it is testimony that the candidate is, according to the voter's informed judgment, capable and trustworthy enough to represent people. A vote cast for someone known to lack those qualities misstates that judgment.

Second, it is shafa'ah, a recommendation. The Qur'an attaches a share of the consequences to both good and bad recommendations (4:85). Supporting a deserving person can therefore bring a share in the resulting good. Helping an undeserving person into office can bring a share in the wrong made possible through that support.

Third, the vote is wakalah, appointing an agent or representative. It does not concern only the voter's private property, where he alone might bear the loss. The representative acts in matters involving the community's shared rights. Reckless appointment therefore affects others as well as the voter.

The criticism is directed against treating elections as mere contests of winning and losing. Money, pressure, casual friendships and promises cannot turn an unfit candidate into a fit one. A voter who knowingly endorses the unworthy participates in false testimony, an unjust recommendation and misuse of shared authority at once.

The resulting duty is investigation. Men and women should consider the candidate's competence, suitability, honesty and reliability before voting. Negligence or indifference does not make the choice morally empty. The explanation praises support for a worthy person and warns of responsibility for the predictable wrongdoing of an unworthy one.

### What makes justice part of the covenant?

The previous verse explained the inward pledge of hearing and obeying (5:7). Here that pledge takes the form of fair treatment. A person must give another what is actually deserved, rather than what anger or affection would prefer.

Bitter memories are a particular test. They can make unfairness feel like loyalty to a past injury. The verse requires the believer to resist that movement and remain faithful to Allah. Justice toward an enemy is not forgetfulness of the wrong. It is refusal to answer it with a fresh violation of the covenant.

### In short

- Stand for Allah, not for reputation or faction, and give honest evidence.
- Neither affection for friends nor hatred of enemies permits injustice.
- True witnesses have a duty to speak, while authorities have a duty not to harass or needlessly burden them.
- Certificates, examination marks and votes can all carry the responsibility of testimony.
- Allah knows what is actually done. Fairness must therefore govern both public decisions and private motives.

9.text:
Allah answers faithful obedience with a promise: "Allah has promised those who believe and do good ˹His˺ forgiveness and a great reward". Belief and righteous action are joined, and the promised outcome joins pardon with Paradise. The declaration gives hope after the demand for difficult, impartial justice.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah has promised"** makes the assurance His own. It is not a wish based on uncertain human approval. Allah does not fail His promise.

**"those who believe and do good"** describes people who believe in Allah and His messengers and act in obedience. A gloss specifies belief in Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an, together with the duties between servants and their Lord. Accepting Allah's guidance must bear fruit in conduct.

**"˹His˺ forgiveness"** promises pardon for sins. One explanation describes their sins being forgiven in this world. The promise is not limited to overlooking outward faults before other people. It concerns their standing before Allah.

**"and a great reward"** means Paradise. The reward is an expression of Allah's generosity and mercy toward His believing servants.

### Is Paradise purchased by good deeds?

The explanation distinguishes a cause from an independent entitlement. Good deeds are the way Allah has appointed toward His mercy, pardon and acceptance. They matter, but they do not place Him under a debt payable apart from His favour.

Paradise is therefore entered through His mercy, even though righteous actions are the appointed means of receiving it. The ability to follow that way and the mercy granted at its end both come from Allah. Gratitude, rather than self-sufficiency, is the proper response to the promise.

Allah makes His guidance known through signs and arguments. Those who accept that guidance, rather than evade it, are described as deserving the promised reward. Their response is faith expressed in good action, not simply clever speech about religion.

### In short

- Allah promises forgiveness and Paradise to those whose faith is joined with righteous conduct.
- His promise is dependable, while the reward remains His mercy rather than an independent debt owed to human achievement.
- Good deeds are the means He has appointed toward pardon and acceptance.

10.text:
The contrasting outcome is stated plainly: "As for those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the residents of the Hellfire". Rejection of Allah and His revelations has a consequence different from the forgiveness and reward promised to believing obedience.

### Phrase by phrase

**"As for those who disbelieve"** describes rejection of Allah. The verse does not treat unbelief as equivalent to the faithful response described immediately before it.

**"and deny Our signs"** includes denial of His revelations and the evidence through which His guidance is made known. A gloss specifically names Muhammad ﷺ and the Qur'an as what is being rejected.

**"they are the residents of the Hellfire"** describes enduring residence, not a passing encounter. The explanation compares their attachment to the Fire with the continuing association of a companion with his companion. They enter as a consequence of disbelief and rejection and remain there.

### What does denying a sign involve?

The warning includes encountering Allah's clear argument and answering it with verbal evasions instead of acceptance. Cleverness in speech does not change the truth of what has been shown. Refusing the evidence while obscuring that refusal with words is treated as denial of His signs.

The punishment is explained through Allah's perfect justice, wisdom and judgment. He does not wrong anyone or make a mistaken decision. The contrast with the preceding promise presents both mercy toward believing obedience and justice toward deliberate rejection.

### In short

- Denial concerns Allah and the signs through which His guidance is made known.
- Evasive argument does not turn rejection into acceptance.
- The Fire is described as the abiding outcome of that rejection, under Allah's just judgment.

11.text:
Allah asks believers to remember protection as a gift: "O believers! Remember Allah’s favour upon you: when a people sought to harm you, but He held their hands back from you." An enemy's intention did not become the outcome the enemy wanted. The believers' safety therefore calls for gratitude, obedience and reliance on Allah, not confidence in their own independence.

The reports connect the reminder with more than one attempted attack on the Prophet ﷺ and his community. They should be retained as different accounts rather than forced into a single incident.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O believers! Remember Allah’s favour upon you"** calls for remembrance by both heart and tongue. The addressed believers include Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions. Their safety and deliverance from hostile plans belong among the favours to be acknowledged.

**"when a people sought to harm you"** describes a real intention to attack or kill. The image of hands reaching toward them expresses an attempt to put hostility into action. Several accounts identify different groups or incidents.

**"but He held their hands back from you"** means that Allah prevented the intended harm. His protection included turning the attackers away and placing fear in their hearts. A dangerous situation did not lie beyond His knowledge or power.

**"Be mindful of Allah."** Gratitude for safety must take the form of obeying His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Taqwa, awareness of Allah, is required after deliverance as well as during danger.

**"And in Allah let the believers put their trust"** directs reliance to Him alone for religious and worldly needs. The explanation promises that He suffices for those who trust Him and protects them against the evil plans of others.

### What happened when a man took the Prophet's ﷺ sword?

Abdur-Razzaq records Jabir describing a halt during a journey. People spread out under trees for shade. The Prophet ﷺ hung his weapon on a tree and rested. A bedouin seized it, raised it toward him and asked who could protect him now.

The Prophet ﷺ answered that Allah would protect him. The man repeated his question two or three times and received the same answer. He eventually lowered the sword or returned it to its sheath. With the man sitting beside him, the Prophet ﷺ summoned his Companions and described the encounter. In this account he imposed no punishment on the attacker.

Ma'mar reports that Qatadah connected the event with Arabs who wanted the Prophet ﷺ killed and sent the man for that purpose. Qatadah would then cite this reminder of Allah restraining hostile hands. The story is also mentioned in the Sahih, where the man's name is given as Ghawrath bin Al-Harith.

Another report from Jabir gives a different form of the encounter. Ghawrath ibn al-Harith, a man from Muharib, offered before people of Banu Ghatafan and Muharib to assassinate Muhammad ﷺ. He approached the Prophet ﷺ while the sword lay in his lap and asked to see it. The Prophet ﷺ handed it over.

The man drew it and moved it about, but Allah restrained him whenever he meant to strike. He asked whether the Prophet ﷺ feared him, especially now that he held the weapon. The Prophet ﷺ replied that Allah would protect him. Ghawrath put the sword back into its sheath and returned it. This account also connects the verse with the failed attack.

The differences concern how the weapon came into the man's hands and how the encounter unfolded. The point they share is reliance on Allah in an immediate danger and the failure of the intended harm. The details need not be silently merged.

### What was the plot involving Bani An-Nadir?

Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar, Mujahid and 'Ikrimah connect the verse with a plot by Bani An-Nadir. The Prophet ﷺ had gone to them seeking help with the blood money for two people killed by Muslims. While he sat beneath a wall, they planned to drop a stone onto his head.

The task was assigned to 'Amr bin Jihash bin Ka'b. Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ of the plan. He left for Madinah, and his Companions followed afterward. The intended attack was therefore prevented before it could be carried out.

The account goes on to say that Allah commanded the Prophet ﷺ to expel Bani An-Nadir. He besieged their area and required them to leave Madinah. This is the continuation attached to that particular report, not part of the separate sword incident.

### Are other groups mentioned?

A brief explanation identifies the people intending harm as Banu Qurayzah. Another names Quraysh. Neither supplies a detailed incident alongside that identification. These should remain distinct notices rather than being turned into an invented combined narrative.

The variety of accounts does not change the practical instruction. Believers are to recognise that Allah protected them from an attack their opponents intended. Remembering deliverance should deepen their dependence on Him and their fidelity to His commands.

### What is the proper response to protection?

The verse does not end with praise of the believers' strength. It ends with mindfulness and trust. Safety can be received wrongly if it produces forgetfulness, pride or the assumption that obedience no longer matters.

The instructed response holds the past and present together. Remember the favour already received, fulfil the duties now required and entrust what lies ahead to Allah. The protection of the Messenger ﷺ is among the concrete reminders through which the community is taught that reliance.

### In short

- Allah's prevention of an intended attack is a favour to remember with heart and tongue.
- Reports connect the verse with the man who took the Prophet's ﷺ sword and with the plot of Bani An-Nadir. Brief glosses name other groups without supplying further detail.
- The accounts retain their differences while sharing the theme of harm restrained by Allah.
- Gratitude for deliverance means continued obedience and reliance on Allah in both religious and worldly affairs.

12.text:
Allah recalls an earlier community's pledge so that believers understand the seriousness of their own: "Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel and appointed twelve leaders from among them". The covenant required prayer, payment of the poor due, faith in the messengers, support for them and sincere spending for Allah. His help, forgiveness and Paradise were promised in connection with those duties, not merely with ancestry.

The verse ends by warning that disbelief after accepting such a covenant is a deliberate departure from a clearly marked way. The appointment of leaders made the commitment a shared responsibility with practical oversight, not simply a declaration left without anyone to uphold it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Allah made a covenant with the Children of Israel"** recalls a binding promise to obey Him. One explanation includes their acknowledgment in the Torah of Muhammad ﷺ, worship of Allah alone and rejection of partners with Him. The covenant has definite requirements, which the verse proceeds to name.

**"and appointed twelve leaders from among them"** means one representative from each of their twelve tribes. Each undertook responsibility for his people as well as for himself. The narration shifts from speaking about Allah to His saying "We", drawing attention to His appointment. Some glosses call the twelve messengers or kings, while the main explanation describes tribal chiefs responsible for keeping the pledge.

**"and ˹then˺ said, “I am truly with you."** promises Allah's protection, assistance and support if the covenant is fulfilled. It also reminds them that He watches everything connected with it. Their intentions, private plans and outward actions cannot escape His knowledge.

**"If you establish prayer, pay alms-tax"** names salah and zakah, worship and the obligatory due from wealth. Prayer is to be maintained properly, not merely acknowledged. Giving the poor due discharges rights others have in one's possessions. These duties were laid upon the people of Musa (Moses) before the coming of this community.

**"believe in My messengers, support them"** requires accepting all the messengers Allah sends, honouring them and helping their work of true guidance. A gloss includes armed assistance against an enemy within that support. Belief is not to be restricted to a preferred messenger while later messengers are rejected.

**"and lend to Allah a good loan"** calls for spending in His cause with a sincere heart. The money is not given to supply a need in Allah. It is called a loan to assure the giver of a return. Its goodness includes sincerity and giving what is valued rather than seeking an easy disposal of worthless things.

**"I will certainly forgive your sins and admit you into Gardens under which rivers flow."** promises pardon and entry into Paradise. Sins are covered and erased rather than punished. One gloss qualifies the sins mentioned as other than the enormities. The Gardens include dwellings and trees with rivers beneath them, and a fuller gloss names water, milk, wine and honey. The promise joins removal of what is feared with attainment of what is hoped for.

**"And whoever among you disbelieves afterwards has truly strayed from the Right Way.”"** warns against rejection after accepting the pledge. Al-sawa' originally conveys the middle way. Here it is the clear road of guidance leading to Paradise, from which the covenant-breaker knowingly turns aside. The wording makes the assurance solemn through the form of an oath attached to its conditions.

### Why place this after the believers' own covenant?

The earlier reminder calls Muslims back to their declaration of hearing and obeying (5:7). The statement of faith that Allah alone is worthy of worship and Muhammad ﷺ is His Messenger binds its speaker to obedience. The following command requires justice toward both friend and enemy (5:8). The reminder of protection shows another side of Allah's favour (5:11).

The present account shows that taking a covenant is not unique to Muslims. Earlier communities received duties, promises and warnings too. Their history therefore gives the present hearer a reason to take the same kind of commitment seriously.

Help is connected with taqwa, awareness of Allah, and tawakkul, trust in Him. The discussion stresses that victory does not depend on outward equipment alone. Fear of Allah keeps a person faithful when breaking a pledge would otherwise be tempting. Trust in Him prevents just treatment of an enemy from appearing pointless merely because it is not immediate revenge.

The argument also answers the fear that tolerance will simply allow a defeated enemy to recover and attack again. Justice and courtesy, joined to faithfulness and reliance on Allah, may instead draw hearts toward Islam. This is the religious basis of the confidence described, not a claim that every outward arrangement guarantees safety by itself. Iqbal's poetic image expresses it by calling for the spirit of Badr if people seek help like the angelic help of that occasion.

### What were the twelve chiefs responsible for?

Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad bin Ishaq connect their selection with Musa's campaign against the powerful people in Palestine. Allah commanded a representative to be chosen from each tribe. They pledged obedience to Allah, His messenger and His Book on behalf of their tribes.

Representation did not release the rest of the people from duty. The chiefs were to obey themselves and help ensure their people's obedience. The collective arrangement supported continued prayer, payment of others' rights, allegiance to the messengers and spending for the religion.

This reveals the difference between the use of family knowledge in administration and a claim of inherited superiority. A familiar member of a group may understand its circumstances and enjoy its trust. Giving him responsibility can help maintain order without declaring his ancestry better before Allah.

The Prophet's ﷺ final Hajj address rejected superiority based on being Arab rather than non-Arab, white rather than black, or of a supposedly higher caste. Membership in Islam brought brotherhood. Jami's poetic reminder makes the same point: the servant travelling in love must leave boasts of parentage behind. Being someone's son does not establish spiritual rank.

Ancestry can therefore help identify people for practical arrangements without becoming the measure of their worth. The tribal structure is used here to secure responsibility, not to replace obedience with privilege.

### How does the account of twelve springs illustrate this?

When the Children of Israel faced shortage of water, Musa prayed and was commanded to strike a rock with his staff. Twelve springs flowed, providing for the twelve communities. The Qur'an mentions their division into tribes and the springs that supplied them (7:160).

The arrangement gave each group its provision and reduced grounds for conflict. It is another example of recognising social groupings for a useful purpose rather than treating them as competing spiritual ranks. The same practical concern explains the appointment of a chief for each tribe.

### Which twelve leaders represented the Ansar?

At 'Aqabah the Prophet ﷺ likewise received a pledge through twelve leaders from the Ansar, the helpers of Madinah. Three represented Aws and nine represented Khazraj. They undertook allegiance and obedience on behalf of their people.

From Aws were Usayd bin Al-Hudayr and Sa'd bin Khaythamah. The third is given as Rifa'ah bin 'Abdul-Mundhir, with Abu Al-Haytham bin At-Tayhan named as an alternative in the account.

The Khazraj representatives included the two Sa'ds, Sa'd bin 'Ubadah and Sa'd bin Ar-Rabi', and 'Ubadah bin As-Samit. Also named are Abu Umamah As'ad bin Zurarah, Al-Bara' bin Ma'rur and Rafi' bin Malik bin Al-'Ajlan. Completing the nine are 'Abdullah bin Rawahah, Al-Mundhir bin 'Umar bin Khunays and 'Abdullah bin 'Amr bin Haram.

Ibn Ishaq records Ka'b bin Malik's poem naming these men. Their representative pledge is given as a parallel to the earlier appointment, not as a claim that the two events were identical in every detail.

### Must twelve rulers follow one another without interruption?

A report from Jabir ibn Samurah in Al-Bukhari and Muslim speaks of people's affairs remaining sustained while twelve ruling authorities lead them. The discussion cautions that the report does not state that all twelve must succeed one another continuously. They may be separated by intervals.

The first four are named in their order: Abu Bakr, 'Umar al-Faruq, 'Uthman al-Ghani and 'Ali al-Murtada. After an interval, 'Umar ibn 'Abdul-'Aziz is described as accepted by the community as a fifth rightly guided ruler. The account does not supply a completed list of twelve, and one should not be constructed from outside it.

The comparison draws attention to the recurring number while retaining the limited claim actually made. It is not a reason to force every later ruler into an invented sequence.

### Why are prayer and zakah mentioned before faith in the messengers?

Iman, faith, is foundational to action. The order here does not reverse that relationship. The explanation distinguishes duties already to be performed from the future arrival of further messengers. Prayer and zakah were immediate obligations, while accepting and supporting later messengers would be tested as they came.

The passage also stresses that prayer and zakah were not invented for this final community. They belonged to earlier prophetic guidance, not only to the Children of Israel but to the successive revealed laws. The covenant names basic religious responsibilities that join worship of Allah to the rights of other people.

The promise of Paradise therefore rests on faithfulness, not racial connection. A community cannot preserve the claim to Allah's support while discarding the duties attached to that claim.

### What makes a loan to Allah good?

The good loan is expenditure offered sincerely for His pleasure, without a concealed worldly bargain. Giving only what is unwanted while retaining everything valued contradicts the generous spirit described. The image of a loan assures the giver that the expenditure will not be lost.

A loan is ordinarily expected to be returned under law, custom and conscience. Applying that language to spending for Allah strengthens confidence in His reward. The giver is encouraged to regard the return as certain, though its granting is Allah's generosity.

Zakah has already been named separately. The good loan therefore includes other charity and communal needs, rather than merely repeating the same obligation. Paying zakah does not settle every financial responsibility that can arise among Muslims.

The discussion gives examples such as building a needed mosque or supporting religious education when the authorities do not provide it. Institutions teaching children and adults still need resources. Their needs cannot automatically be dismissed by saying that one's annual zakah has been paid.

### How do individual and communal financial duties differ?

Zakah is described as fard 'ayn, an obligation resting upon each individual who owes it. Other needs may be fard kifayah, a collective obligation. If enough people fulfil a collective duty, the remainder are released from its burden. If nobody undertakes it, the neglect leaves everyone responsible.

The criticism here is directed at two failures. Some people do not pay zakah at all, or pay it without properly calculating the full amount. Others do pay it but imagine that no further financial duty can ever arise. The passage particularly describes the hardship faced by people maintaining religious schools with insufficient support.

It also criticises the habit of offering only zakah money whenever a mosque or educational institution needs help, without recognising distinct duties of support beyond zakah. The point is to preserve the difference between the obligatory due already named and the wider charitable expenditure named afterward. The verse is not reduced to a single payment that ends concern for every communal need.

### What happens if the covenant is rejected?

The promised forgiveness and lasting comfort depend on fulfilling the stated responsibilities. Rejection after the pledge means turning away from instructions already made clear. The wrong is therefore not merely lack of information but departure from acknowledged guidance.

A brief report says that they disbelieved except for five. It supplies neither the names nor a fuller explanation of that count. Its qualification is retained without using it to construct an additional historical account.

The warning prepares for the next verse's description of the covenant's breach and its consequences. The promise and warning are parts of the same offer, not two unrelated messages.

### In short

- The covenant required worship, payment of others' rights, acceptance and support of the messengers, and sincere spending for Allah.
- Twelve tribal representatives were made responsible for helping their people keep it. Practical organisation does not make ancestry a measure of spiritual superiority.
- Prayer and zakah belonged to earlier revelation too. Faithfulness, not lineage, is the basis of the promised help and Paradise.
- The good loan includes financial duties beyond zakah, including communal needs that someone must fulfil.
- Rejecting the covenant after accepting it is a knowing departure from the way of guidance.

13.text:
The consequence of breaking the covenant is stated directly: "But for breaking their covenant We condemned them and hardened their hearts." The verse describes punishment that reaches understanding and character, not only outward circumstances. Distortion of scripture, neglect of its demands and repeated treachery follow that inward hardness.

Yet the instruction to the Prophet ﷺ does not simply mirror their wrongdoing with contempt. It ends by commanding pardon and good conduct. Their failure does not release him from the conduct Allah loves.

### Phrase by phrase

**"But for breaking their covenant We condemned them"** makes their breach the cause of the punishment. The grammatical form reinforces that causal connection. La'nah, condemnation or curse, is explained as removal from Allah's mercy and its effects. Another gloss includes the imposition of a capitation tax among the punishments described.

**"and hardened their hearts."** Their hearts became resistant to faith and good advice. Words of guidance no longer found a receptive place. This is a spiritual consequence of disobedience, not a claim that sincere obedience first caused an innocent heart to be rejected.

**"They distorted the words of the Scripture"** includes changing words, their recitation or their intended meanings. They moved revelation away from its proper setting and interpreted it to suit desire. Particular examples include the Torah's description of Muhammad ﷺ and its ruling on stoning married people who commit illicit intercourse.

**"and neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold."** Forgetting here includes deliberate abandonment in practice. The explanation particularly mentions the instruction to follow Muhammad ﷺ and make his description known. Possessing a text is not the same as acting upon its reminder.

**"You ˹O Prophet˺ will always find deceit on their part, except for a few."** The Prophet ﷺ would continue discovering broken promises and plots against him and his Companions. Mujahid mentions the attempt to kill him. A gloss identifies Banu Qurayzah in this connection. The exception is real: 'Abdullah Ibn Salam and other sincere believers are given as examples of those who did not share the betrayal.

**"But pardon them and bear with them."** He is told to overlook wrongdoing and refrain from taking them to task in the manner covered by this command. The instruction calls for restraint rather than letting knowledge of their conduct corrupt his own.

**"Indeed, Allah loves the good-doers"** gives the positive reason. Kindness and moral excellence remain loved by Allah even when their immediate recipients are difficult or unresponsive. The believer's conduct has a value before Him beyond the reaction it receives.

### How can punishment take place within the heart?

The discussion distinguishes visible punishment from inward punishment. Visible examples include destructive stones or the overturning of land. Inward punishment concerns damaged judgment and feeling, leaving a person increasingly unable to recognise truth or respond to it.

Surah al-Mutaffifin describes the stain placed upon hearts by wrongdoing. A report from the Prophet ﷺ explains the process through a dark mark left by sin. At first the mark is painful and noticeable, like a stain on clean cloth. Repentance and a resolve to leave the wrongdoing remove it.

If the person becomes careless and continues sinning, the marks accumulate until darkness covers the heart. The image then becomes that of an overturned vessel: what is poured toward it cannot remain inside. Good counsel cannot settle there because the disposition receiving it has become resistant.

The person may eventually reverse moral judgments, calling a vice a virtue or a defect a merit. This is already a punishment within worldly life, before the final judgment. Repetition makes the wrongdoing easier to repeat.

Some early teachers express the corresponding pattern on both sides. One good action is rewarded with tawfiq, Allah-given ability, to perform another. One sin can draw the heart toward another sin. Obedience and disobedience each acquire a momentum, which is why a first failure should lead to repentance rather than indifference.

### How does distortion replace the covenant?

When understanding becomes corrupt, the person no longer allows revelation to correct desire. Instead, revelation is made to appear to support whatever is desired. Words may be changed, passages detached from their meanings or explanations shaped to avoid their demands. The discussion also notes that some acknowledgments of textual alteration have come from European Christians themselves, without supplying further examples here.

The wider warning concerns a community constructing its own religion while retaining a revealed name. Prayer becomes a subject of irrelevant disputes rather than obedience. People seek salvation without discharging the rights of others. Worldly activity is called service of truth, and ordinary self-interested expenditure is given religious excuses.

Once that pattern dominates, the guidance is no longer being followed. The community recognises the language of its desires more readily than the demands of its covenant. Death then brings people before Allah despite the religious labels they used to justify themselves.

This is why the exception for a few must not be ignored. The verse does not erase those who remain faithful or accept the truth. Its judgment concerns breach and distortion, not a refusal to recognise any sincere person among the addressed people.

### Why command pardon after exposing treachery?

A natural reaction to repeated betrayal would be contempt and refusal to have anything further to do with the offenders. The verse directs the Prophet ﷺ toward a better response. Courtesy may reach a person whom argument alone has failed to move.

Even where that hope is not realised, maintaining one's own good conduct remains necessary. Another person's hard heart is not a reason to spoil one's own character. The good action still brings the doer nearer to Allah's pleasure.

An early saying puts the principle in terms of responding to disobedience with obedience. When someone violates Allah's command in treating a believer, the finest response is to keep Allah's command in treating that person. Pardon may gather hearts around truth and become a means of guidance.

A differing legal account is also recorded. Qatadah regards this command as abrogated by the later instruction to fight those who do not believe in Allah or the Last Day. Another gloss calls it superseded by the sword verse, but its printed reference is malformed. That opinion is preserved without adding a precise verse number from outside the material. The explanation praising pardon and the stated abrogation view should both remain visible.

### In short

- Breach of the covenant brought distance from mercy and hearts resistant to guidance.
- Repeated sin can corrupt judgment, while repentance removes its stain and obedience opens the way to further good.
- Distorting scripture includes bending its meaning to desire and neglecting duties while retaining religious language.
- The faithful few are explicitly excepted. The command to pardon teaches good conduct despite betrayal, alongside a recorded view that the command was later superseded.

14.text:
The warning extends to another scriptural community: "And from those who say, “We are Christians,” We took their covenant". They too abandoned part of what they had been instructed to uphold. The consequence described is hostility and enmity among them, continuing until the final judgment when Allah will disclose and repay their deeds.

The verse therefore distinguishes a religious claim from faithfulness to its obligations. Calling oneself a follower of 'Isa (Jesus) does not by itself fulfil the covenant attached to that claim.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And from those who say, “We are Christians,” We took their covenant"** recalls their pledge in the Gospel. It included worshipping Allah alone, accepting every messenger He sends and following Muhammad ﷺ when he came. The explanation also includes acknowledging and making known his description. A particular gloss identifies Christians of Najran.

**"but they neglected a portion of what they had been commanded to uphold."** They abandoned part of the instruction concerning faith and practice. This is not described merely as failure to remember a sentence. It is a failure to fulfil a binding reminder, like the preceding covenant-breaking.

**"So We let hostility and enmity arise between them until the Day of Judgment"** describes the result of schism and competing desires. One reading places it among Christian sects. Another includes hostility between Jews and Christians. The explanation mentions mutual accusations of unbelief, fighting and destruction as expressions of that enmity.

**"and soon Allah will inform them of all they have done"** threatens final disclosure and repayment. Their opposition, concealed truth, betrayal and hatred will not disappear behind claims of religious loyalty. Allah knows the actions for which they will answer.

### How is the sectarian conflict described?

The account describes groups condemning one another's beliefs and excluding one another from places of worship. It names the Monarchist or Melkite group, Jacobites, Nestorians and Arians. Another gloss mentions the Nestorians of Najran together with Jacobites, Marqusiyya and Melkites.

A brief classification cited through al-Baydawi gives three formulations concerning 'Isa. It describes the Fisturyah, Nestorians, as calling him Allah's son. It describes the Ya'qubiyah, Jacobites, as identifying him with Allah, and the Malka'iyah, Malkites, as treating him as one of the Trinity. These are the classifications supplied in that account, not an independent historical survey of each group's full theology.

The shared objection is to attributing a companion or son to Allah. He is one and self-sufficient, neither born nor begetting, with no equal. The warning concerns claims opposed to that oneness and the conflicts sustained through them.

### What if some nominal Christians appear united?

The discussion answers by distinguishing religious adherence from a merely inherited or national label. It applies the statement about religious dissension to people who continue professing and practising Christianity. Those who have left religion for secular or atheistic commitments are not treated as proof that religious schisms have ended simply because records still call them Christian.

The explanation is about the basis of the hostility being described. If religious commitment has been abandoned, the absence of a particular theological dispute among those people does not answer a statement about divisions within continuing religious adherence. This is the distinction made in the discussion, not a claim about the personal beliefs of every person using a Christian identity today.

### How can neglect harden into a lasting sect?

The inward account describes communities turning from clear, enduring commands to matters of merely local or temporary interest. Dissatisfied with the guidance received, people seek new controversies concerning law, spiritual life or political activity. Worldly desire is then allowed to decide what should count as religion.

Changes may be defended as keeping up with the times or correcting what is imagined to be an incomplete religion. Each new version gathers people with similar preferences. Later generations inherit it and defend it as the sacred possession of their ancestors.

The passage of time then gives the invention an appearance of permanence. Loyalty to the inherited version becomes a religious duty in people's eyes. Hostility to others can even be presented as obedience to Allah. What began as departure from a common covenant becomes a continuing justification for division and violence.

The final judgment exposes that substitution. A venerable name or long history cannot conceal what people actually did with the instruction they received.

### In short

- Christian communities also received a covenant of worship, faith and obedience, and are judged by fidelity rather than their claim alone.
- Neglect of the reminder is linked to continuing hostility and competing sectarian loyalties.
- Inherited custom can be mistaken for revelation and used to sanctify hatred.
- Allah will disclose and repay the deeds hidden behind religious claims.

15.text:
Allah addresses Jews and Christians with the arrival of guidance that exposes concealment without making exposure an end in itself: "O People of the Book! Now Our Messenger has come to you". Muhammad ﷺ makes clear much that had been hidden from earlier scripture, while leaving aside matters whose disclosure would bring no benefit. The verse presents his coming and the clear Book as light from Allah.

The address offers correction as a favour. It restores neglected guidance and removes burdens added under the name of religion. People who sincerely seek Allah's pleasure can follow it out of confusion, while those determined to follow desire may refuse its evidence.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O People of the Book!"** addresses the Jews, recipients of the Torah, and the Christians, recipients of the Gospel. Their connection to earlier revelation makes the call to receive and follow guidance especially direct.

**"Now Our Messenger has come to you"** identifies Muhammad ﷺ as Allah's Messenger. His mission brings clear evidence and a distinction between truth and falsehood. It is not confined to one ethnicity or educational class: Arabs and non-Arabs, the lettered and the unlettered, are all addressed by his message.

**"revealing much of what you have hidden of the Scriptures"** includes explaining alteration, distortion and false claims made about Allah. Specific examples are the description of the Prophet ﷺ and the legal ruling on stoning married people who commit unlawful intercourse. Concealing such instruction does not remove its place in the revelation.

**"and disregarding much."** He does not expose everything that could be exposed. Some disclosure would only humiliate people without advancing guidance. Passing it over is therefore not endorsement of the alteration, but restraint where recounting it would serve no useful purpose.

**"There certainly has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book"** is explained in two closely related ways. One identifies the light as the Prophet ﷺ and the clear Book as the Qur'an. Another describes the Qur'an itself as both illuminating and plain. It makes lawful and unlawful matters clear and supplies guidance for religious and worldly life.

### What concealment is illustrated by the stoning ruling?

Al-Hakim records in his Mustadrak a statement from Ibn 'Abbas connecting the concealed instruction with stoning. Ibn 'Abbas warns that rejecting that ruling would, without the person realising it, amount to rejecting the Qur'an, because it was among the matters whose concealment this verse exposes.

Al-Hakim describes the chain as sahih, authentic, and notes that the two leading collectors did not record it. The attribution and its stated assessment belong with the report. The example shows how the general language about concealed scripture is understood through a particular legal matter.

### How can religion be damaged by both omission and addition?

One error is to remove a demand through distortion or deliberate misinterpretation. The discussion gives the example of treating inherited attachment to ancestral religion as sufficient for salvation, thereby avoiding the need to accept a later prophet.

The other error is to impose restrictions Allah did not appoint. Elaborate details of sacrificial practice are given as an example of burdens created through excessive interpretation rather than commanded by the prophets. A person may therefore lose genuine guidance while becoming increasingly strict about invented requirements.

The Qur'an's corrective role addresses both errors. It renews the obscured teachings and releases people from unnecessary restraints. This is why its exposure is described as light rather than merely accusation. It shows where people had mistaken a path toward divine anger for a path toward Paradise.

Clear reasoning still requires a receptive mind. Evidence can distinguish truth from falsehood, but a person intent on desire can refuse to listen. The saving effect of this light is developed in the following verse through the response of those seeking Allah's pleasure.

### In short

- The Messenger ﷺ brings clear guidance to the People of the Book and to humanity beyond them.
- He exposes concealed instruction where it serves guidance, while passing over disclosure that would only disgrace people.
- The light and clear Book restore neglected duties and remove invented burdens.
- Receiving that correction requires an open mind rather than loyalty to desire or inherited error.

16.text:
The Book's light is effective guidance for a willing response: "through which Allah guides those who seek His pleasure to the ways of peace". Allah brings those people out of darkness and directs them toward a straight way. The change is both a movement away from disbelief and disobedience and a movement into faith, safety and obedience.

### Phrase by phrase

**"through which Allah guides"** refers to the Book just mentioned. Another explanation includes the guidance brought through Muhammad ﷺ together with the Qur'an. The Messenger and revelation are the means, while Allah is the One who grants guidance.

**"those who seek His pleasure"** describes people who believe, act rightly and wish to please Him. A gloss connects this response particularly with accepting His oneness. Guidance is not merely possession of a text while resisting its demands.

**"to the ways of peace"** means ways of safety and righteousness, protecting from punishment and leading to Paradise. Another explanation connects peace, al-Salam, with Allah Himself and understands these as the ways of His religion, Islam.

**"brings them out of darkness and into light by His Will"** means release from disbelief and disobedience into faith and obedience. It happens by His command and permission. The phrase is also explained through the success and grace He grants, not through a claim that the person independently produces divine guidance.

**"and guides them to the Straight Path"** identifies the clear way of Islam. A gloss adds the meaning of keeping them firm upon that religion after they have accepted it. Guidance includes constancy, not only an initial change of direction.

### What do these images promise?

The images of safety, illumination and a straight road describe guidance from different sides. Allah saves people from ruin, removes confusion and shows the clearest course. He protects them from what they fear and brings them toward the good they desire.

That promise belongs to a response seeking His pleasure. Those who accept correction can leave the darkness in which they previously mistook error for guidance. The destination is not simply greater confidence, but a righteous condition and the way leading to Paradise.

### In short

- Allah guides through the revelation and the Messenger ﷺ those who sincerely seek His pleasure.
- Peace means safety and righteousness, while light means faith and obedience instead of their opposites.
- The straight way is Islam, and guidance includes remaining firm upon it by Allah's grace.

17.text:
Allah rejects the claim that a created messenger is himself divine: "Indeed, those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have fallen into disbelief." The answer asks who could prevent Allah from ending the life of 'Isa (Jesus), his mother Maryam (Mary), or everyone on earth. Their dependence upon Him distinguishes them from the One whose authority encompasses all creation.

The verse also answers the argument based on 'Isa's extraordinary birth. Allah creates as He wills. A birth outside the ordinary pattern demonstrates the Creator's power, not the child's divinity.

### Phrase by phrase

**"Indeed, those who say, “Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary,” have fallen into disbelief."** The specific claim is identified in the glosses with the Jacobites. 'Isa is Allah's servant, messenger and creature. Making him Allah contradicts divine oneness, however honoured his place among the messengers.

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Who has the power to prevent Allah if He chose to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, his mother, and everyone in the world all together?”"** asks about the power to resist Allah's will. No one can provide that resistance. If the Messiah possessed divinity, he would not stand helpless before another's power over his own existence.

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between."** All beings and all the resources and wonders of creation belong to Him. His authority is not one portion of a shared rule. Those people whom others worship are themselves within His dominion.

**"He creates whatever He wills."** Allah can create with or without the ordinary means. His creative power is not restricted by the familiar pattern of a father and mother.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything"** affirms the power behind the whole argument. It includes creating beings, rewarding His faithful servants and punishing His enemies. Nothing in creation lies beyond His ability.

### Why mention Maryam with her son?

One explanation draws attention to 'Isa's complete submission. He cannot resist Allah's will concerning himself, nor can he independently protect the mother whose care a good son values so highly. Their close relationship does not give either of them divine independence.

Another explanation sees the joint mention as answering the view of a sect that placed Maryam among three divine beings. The argument defeats that claim along with the claim about her son. Anyone subject to Allah's power over life and death is not a partner in His divinity.

Although the question is framed as a supposition, Maryam's death had already occurred by the time of the Qur'an's revelation. Two explanations are given. Her case may be included under the hypothetical wording primarily directed at 'Isa. Alternatively, the sense is that Allah who had already caused her to die could likewise cause the Messiah and all others to die.

### Does a birth without a father prove divinity?

No. The comparison with Adam directly addresses that reasoning (3:59). Allah created Adam without either father or mother. The explanation also mentions Eve without a mother and 'Isa without a father. The different modes of creation belong to one Creator's power.

If departure from the usual pattern proved that the created being was divine, the same reasoning would have to be applied to these other cases. Instead, the examples show that the ordinary means do not limit Allah. He is worthy of worship because He creates and rules, not because His creatures can restrict how He acts.

### How wide is the argument?

The verse directly names one assertion, that Allah is the Messiah. The explanation says its reasoning also answers other claims against oneness, including divine sonship and a division into three gods. Created beings cannot create or destroy independently of Allah.

The inability to control one's own existence is therefore central. Honouring a messenger does not require giving him the power of the One who sent him. Allah's complete ownership and justice remain undivided.

### In short

- The Messiah and his mother belong to Allah's creation and cannot prevent His will.
- Their dependence refutes making either of them divine or a partner in divine rule.
- Extraordinary birth shows Allah's freedom to create, as the comparison with Adam makes clear.
- All sovereignty and creative power belong to Allah alone.

18.text:
Allah challenges a claim to guaranteed favour: "The Jews and the Christians each say, “We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!”" The response asks why they are punished for their sins if their asserted relationship places them beyond judgment. They are human beings among His creation, subject to forgiveness and punishment rather than protected by an inherited title.

The verse ends where its argument begins: with Allah's authority. He owns all creation, and everyone will return to Him. No community can make its own claim of privilege the rule by which He must judge it.

### Phrase by phrase

**"The Jews and the Christians each say, “We are the children of Allah and His most beloved!”"** describes a claim of special closeness, care and rank. A gloss identifies the Jews of Madinah and Christians of Najran. The claim is also explained as identifying themselves with the prophets they follow and assuming the same favoured status.

**"Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Why then does He punish you for your sins?"** exposes the contradiction in their claim to assured exemption. The explanations mention punishment in worldly life and the threatened Fire in the Hereafter. A specific gloss recalls calf-worship lasting forty days. Their own experience of accountability contradicts the absolute privilege they assert.

**"No! You are only humans like others of His Own making."** places them among the children of Adam. They are created servants, not beings whose relationship to Allah removes them from the common judgment of good and evil.

**"He forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills."** His pardon is grace and His punishment is justice. Neither can be compelled by communal self-description. One gloss applies pardon to those who repent from the rejected beliefs described and punishment to those who die persisting in them.

**"To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and everything in between."** all creation and its resources lie under His ownership and control. There is no separate domain in which a group can claim immunity from Him.

**"And to Him is the final return.”"** means the final journey of believers and disbelievers alike ends before Allah. He judges His servants with perfect justice and does not err in that judgment.

### Did they mean literal children in the same sense as their claim about 'Isa?

The explanation distinguishes the claims. Christians did not generally call themselves Allah's children in the same sense in which they made that assertion about 'Isa (Jesus). For themselves, the language concerned nearness, compassion and care, as though Allah's relationship to them were that of a father to favoured children.

A statement associated with their scripture calls Isra'il the firstborn. Some members of the People of the Book who later accepted Islam explained such wording as an expression of honour in the speech of that time, not literal divine parentage. Misreading the expression changes its meaning.

Similarly, words attributed to 'Isa about returning to his father and their father are explained as referring to his Lord and their Lord. Language of closeness cannot establish either literal sonship or guaranteed salvation regardless of conduct.

The Qur'anic answer addresses the privilege they draw from that language. If their special love meant that punishment could never reach them, the punishment for their sins would be inexplicable. The argument concerns their claim to exemption, not an independent theory about how every human parent behaves.

### How can the gifts to earlier believers be misunderstood by descendants?

A community receiving a prophet and scripture may gain help, victory, pardon and the promise of Paradise through sincere submission. In the earlier generation those gifts correspond to its actual response. Later generations may inherit the communal identity without preserving the obedience.

The error is then to treat the identity itself as a guarantee. What was received through faithful action becomes imagined as a racial or national entitlement. People assume the same blessings will continue whatever they do.

The discussion uses a community's fortunes in this world as a warning against that confidence. It argues that continued defeat and humiliation should force a scriptural community to question its claim to automatic divine favour, even when its numbers are large. It presents worldly help and ascendancy as signs within this covenant argument, not as a new measurement of every individual's worth through wealth or power.

The purpose is to remove complacency. A group that disregards the responsibilities of revelation cannot confidently claim that its name alone assures honour in the Hereafter. The final decision remains Allah's, not a status conferred by the group's own description of itself.

### In short

- Claims of divine sonship or special love do not remove accountability for sin.
- The language of honour and closeness must not be turned into literal parentage or inherited immunity.
- Gifts received by faithful ancestors do not guarantee the same outcome to descendants who abandon their conduct.
- All people are Allah's creation and return to His just judgment, receiving pardon through His grace rather than through self-awarded privilege.

19.text:
The People of the Book are told that the long absence of a messenger has ended: "Our Messenger has indeed come to you, making things clear to you after an interval between the messengers". Muhammad ﷺ brings the explanation, good news and warning that the people need. They can no longer meet his message with the excuse that no one came to guide them.

His coming is both a favour and a reason for responsibility. Allah sends guidance before calling people to account, and He has the power to reward those who follow it and punish those who reject it. Belonging to a community associated with an earlier scripture does not replace a person's response to the messenger who has now arrived.

### Phrase by phrase

**"O People of the Book!"** addresses Jews and Christians, the people of the Torah and Gospel. Their scriptures and religious inheritance do not make the new explanation unnecessary.

**"Our Messenger has indeed come to you"** identifies Muhammad ﷺ as Allah's Messenger and the final Prophet. No prophet or messenger will come after him. His mission reaches people at a time of urgent need for renewed clarity.

**"making things clear to you after an interval between the messengers"** describes a fatrah, a period in which the sending of messengers was suspended. The word carries the idea of an activity slackening or ceasing. Here it refers to the interval between 'Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad ﷺ. He clarifies the religious commands and prohibitions that people need to follow.

**"so you do not say, “There has never come to us a deliverer of good news or a warner.”"** removes the proposed excuse of having received no message. The good news concerns Allah's reward and Paradise. The warning concerns punishment and Hell. The wording emphatically denies the absence of such a messenger as an available excuse after his arrival.

**"Now there has come to you a deliverer of good news and a warner."** answers that claim directly. The same Messenger ﷺ brings both encouragement and accountability. A person must respond to the message rather than choose only its comforting or only its frightening part.

**"And Allah is Most Capable of everything"** includes sending His messengers and bringing about the consequences they announce. Ibn Jarir explains it through His power to punish disobedience and reward obedience. Nothing in either task lies beyond Him.

### How long was the interval?

The reports give different figures. Abu 'Uthman An-Nahdi and Qatadah are reported as giving six hundred years, and Al-Bukhari records that figure from Salman Al-Farisi. A separate report from Qatadah gives five hundred and sixty years. Ma'mar gives five hundred and forty. Other accounts give five hundred, 569, or six hundred and twenty.

One proposed reconciliation distinguishes solar from lunar reckoning. The discussion compares six hundred solar years with the longer lunar count, noting a difference of about three years in every hundred. It illustrates that distinction through the people of the Cave, whose stay is given as three hundred years with nine added (18:25).

That explanation concerns the particular difference between the corresponding solar and lunar totals. It need not be turned into a claim that every reported figure has thereby become identical. The main point does not depend on selecting one precise number: a substantial interval separated the two messengers.

Ibn 'Abbas is also reported as describing about seventeen hundred years between Musa (Moses) and 'Isa. In that account, prophets continued to come throughout the earlier period, with a thousand sent among the Children of Israel, besides those sent elsewhere. The later interval is distinguished by the suspension of that succession. The figures are reported estimates, not a new chronological calculation.

### Was there a prophet between 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ?

Abu Hurayrah reports in Al-Bukhari's Sahih that the Prophet ﷺ declared his special closeness to the son of Maryam because no prophet stood between them. The teaching is also cited from Al-Bukhari and Muslim. It identifies 'Isa as the last prophet to the Children of Israel and Muhammad ﷺ as the final prophet and messenger among Adam's descendants.

The three messengers mentioned in Surah Ya Sin are explained here as envoys sent by 'Isa. In that explanation they are messengers in the ordinary sense of people carrying a message, not additional prophets who interrupt the interval.

There are also different treatments of Khalid bin Sinan. Al-Quda'i and others are reported as placing a prophet of that name after 'Isa. The explicit hadith of no prophet between 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ is used to reject that chronology. Another explanation, cited through Shihab, accepts Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Arabi as a prophet but places him before 'Isa, not within the interval. These positions should remain distinct.

### Why was the arrival such a great favour?

The period is described as one of widespread religious alteration, idolatry, fire worship and devotion to the cross. Injustice and ignorance had spread, while only a small number remained faithful to the teachings received through earlier prophets. Examples mentioned include some Jewish teachers, Christian religious figures and Sabian monks.

The few remaining faithful people prevent the description from becoming a claim that every individual was identical. Nevertheless, the general need for clear guidance was great. The message brought people from confusion toward a clear law and a known direction of worship.

'Iyad bin Himar Al-Mujash'i relates a speech recorded by Ahmad in which the Prophet ﷺ conveyed what Allah had taught him. Allah had created His servants inclined toward worship of Him alone. Devils then diverted them, made them forbid what He had permitted and commanded them to associate others with Him without authority.

The report describes Allah looking upon the people of the earth, Arabs and non-Arabs, with displeasure except for a few among the Children of Israel. Muslim's wording describes the exception as a few among the People of the Book. It then presents the Messenger's ﷺ sending as a test for him and for those reached through him.

### What support and instruction does that report describe?

The Book given to the Prophet ﷺ is described as one that water cannot wash away, enduring rather than dependent on a vulnerable written surface. He is described as reciting it asleep and awake. The emphasis is on the lasting gift and his relation to it.

The report also relates a command to confront and destroy the hostile power of Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ feared that they would crush his head. Allah promised to drive them out as they had driven him out, support him in battle and provide for him as he spent upon his companions. It describes one force being supported by five like it and commands him to fight disobedient opponents with those who obeyed him. This belongs to the particular conflict narrated, not an independent command for a reader to attack others.

The speech then gives portraits of the people of Paradise and the Fire. Among the former are a just ruler who is prosperous and charitable, a person merciful to relatives and Muslims, and a poor person with dependants who is forgiving and charitable. Justice, compassion and generosity belong to the moral world the message builds.

The report announces five kinds associated with the Fire. Its translated wording groups the details unevenly, but it describes a weak person without religious restraint, unprincipled followers, a person treacherous even in small matters, and someone who continually schemes against another's family or wealth. It also mentions the miser or liar and the foul-mouthed person. The warning is preserved without inventing a tidier list than the supplied wording provides.

### What is said about people unreached during the interval?

The discussion asks about people who had no prophet, no deputy of a prophet and no preserved law available to them. It sees room for excuse and hope of forgiveness, while attaching the condition that they did not practise shirk, associating partners with Allah.

Jurists differ about the people of the fatrah and whether they are forgiven. The majority view described here inclines toward hope for those who adhered to whatever remained for them of the religion of Musa or 'Isa, even where its transmission was imperfect, provided they did not reject Allah's oneness or embrace associationism.

The reason given for the condition is that oneness can be recognised through reflection, rather than depending entirely on a transmitted legal detail. This is the position and reasoning supplied in the discussion, not a claim that the complex question admits no scholarly disagreement.

### Did possession of the Torah and Gospel already remove every excuse?

The question arises because the addressed communities had books and teachers. Why speak of the absence of guidance if those remained? The answer offered is that alteration and inserted narratives had obscured the original instruction so severely that the available forms did not serve as uncorrupted guidance.

The discussion does not make the survival of an original manuscript somewhere logically impossible. It notes that Ibn Taymiyyah and others wrote of original copies surviving in particular places. A possible copy unknown or inaccessible to most people does not, on this argument, settle what guidance they actually received.

The new Messenger ﷺ removes that uncertainty by making the message clear to those he addresses. Whatever excuse the earlier interval might have allowed cannot simply be carried over unchanged after his explanation arrives.

### How is the transformation of his hearers evidence of his mission?

The explanation points to a people immersed in the ignorance of the period, with stubborn habits and little access to sound knowledge. Through the Prophet's ﷺ teaching and company, they became examples and teachers in conduct, learning, worship and social dealings within a short time.

It illustrates the change through a physician treating a nearly hopeless patient without ordinary instruments or medicines. The patient not only recovers but becomes a capable healer of others. Such a result points to the extraordinary ability of the physician. In the same way, the reform of the Prophet's ﷺ hearers is offered as a public sign of the strength of his message.

The argument does not reduce his mission to a single outward achievement. It draws attention to the breadth of the change in knowledge, actions, character and relationships. The benefit of revelation becomes visible in people who then carry its guidance to others.

### Who is promised Paradise?

No community possesses Paradise as a native homeland, nor is Hell assigned merely by racial identity. The final reckoning concerns persons and their deeds. Allah sends people who reveal the realities of the test, announce reward and warn of punishment.

The response that matters is to support and follow that guidance. A claim to belong to a favoured group cannot replace it. This is why the direct address to the People of the Book ends not in reassurance based on ancestry, but in the removal of an excuse and the reminder of Allah's power.

### In short

- Muhammad ﷺ came after a substantial interval in the sending of prophets, bringing clear instruction, good news and warning.
- The reports differ over the interval's length, but the explicit teaching states that no prophet came between him and 'Isa.
- The message was a great favour in a time of altered guidance and widespread ignorance. Its arrival also removes the excuse that no messenger has come.
- The fate of unreached people is discussed with qualifications and disagreement, not reduced to a blanket claim about every individual.
- Final reward rests on the response to Allah's guidance, not on inherited communal privilege.

20.text:
Before calling his people to a difficult duty, Musa (Moses) recalls the gifts they have already received: "O my people! Remember Allah’s favours upon you when He raised prophets from among you, made you sovereign". Prophetic guidance, freedom after oppression and exceptional provisions all call for gratitude. The reminder prepares them to trust the One who has repeatedly helped them.

The account gives a concrete example of the covenant discussed earlier. The Children of Israel had promised obedience, yet their response to the coming command would test whether past blessings had produced lasting faithfulness. Remembering favour must therefore affect what they are prepared to do next.

### Phrase by phrase

**"And ˹remember˺ when Moses said to his people"** directs attention to Musa, Allah's servant and messenger to whom He spoke. He is named in the account as the son of 'Imran. His address comes as prophetic counsel, preparing his people for the command to enter the Holy Land.
